questions.question: What are Spring Boot Starters, how do they work internally, and how would you build a custom starter?
questions.title: Spring Boot Starters: What They Do and How to Build One
questions.direct_answer: A **Spring Boot Starter** is an **opinionated dependency descriptor** — an essentially empty Maven/Gradle artifact that pulls in a curated, version-aligned set of transitive dependencies plus **auto-configuration** that wires sensible defaults. Internally, starters rely on two mechanisms: **BOM-managed versions** via `spring-boot-dependencies` and **auto-configuration classes** listed in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (Spring Boot 2.7+). To build a custom starter, you create two modules: `*-spring-boot-autoconfigure` (contains `@AutoConfiguration` classes with `@ConditionalOn*` guards and `@ConfigurationProperties`) and `*-spring-boot-starter` (the empty 'marketing' artifact that consumers add). Conditionals ensure safe behavior when optional libs are absent and let users override defaults.

sections.title: A Starter Is an Empty POM with Strong Opinions
sections.content:
A **Spring Boot Starter** is a **dependency aggregator**: a Maven/Gradle artifact that pulls in a cohesive set of transitive dependencies you'd typically use together, all at **versions tested to work together** via the `spring-boot-dependencies` BOM.

A starter has three roles: **dependency grouping** (one line gets you Spring MVC + Tomcat + Jackson + validation), **version alignment** (the BOM pins all transitive versions to a tested combination), and **auto-configuration** (many starters transitively pull autoconfigure JARs that activate when libraries or beans are detected on the classpath).

**Naming conventions matter for discovery**.
- Official starters use `spring-boot-starter-*` (e.g. `spring-boot-starter-web`, `spring-boot-starter-data-redis`).
- Third-party starters use `<project>-spring-boot-starter` (e.g. `camunda-bpm-spring-boot-starter`).
- The reversed naming for third parties signals 'this is not maintained by the Spring team' and prevents namespace squatting.

The **value to a team** is convention plus consistency: every new microservice depends on the same internal `acme-spring-boot-starter` and immediately gets standardized logging, tracing, metrics, and security baselines. The cost is hidden complexity — starters pull dozens of transitive dependencies and auto-configurations that are evaluated even when unused.

sections.title: Starter Anatomy — Empty POM to Wired Beans
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    UserApp["Your application"]
    Starter["spring-boot-starter-web (empty POM)"]
    Mvc["spring-webmvc"]
    Jackson["jackson-databind"]
    Tomcat["spring-boot-starter-tomcat"]
    AutoConf["spring-boot-autoconfigure"]
    Imports["AutoConfiguration.imports"]
    MvcAutoConf["WebMvcAutoConfiguration"]
    JacksonAutoConf["JacksonAutoConfiguration"]
    TomcatAutoConf["EmbeddedTomcatAutoConfiguration"]
    ClassCheck{"MVC class on classpath?"}
    BeansCheck{"User bean already defined?"}
    Wire["Register DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, MessageConverters"]
    Skip["Skip auto-config; use user bean"]

    UserApp -->|depends on| Starter
    Starter --> Mvc
    Starter --> Jackson
    Starter --> Tomcat
    Starter --> AutoConf
    AutoConf --> Imports
    Imports --> MvcAutoConf
    Imports --> JacksonAutoConf
    Imports --> TomcatAutoConf
    MvcAutoConf -->|ConditionalOnClass| ClassCheck
    ClassCheck -->|yes| BeansCheck
    ClassCheck -->|no| Skip
    BeansCheck -->|no| Wire
    BeansCheck -->|yes| Skip
```

sections.title: How Auto-Configuration Actually Fires
sections.content:
**The startup sequence**
- `@SpringBootApplication` triggers `@EnableAutoConfiguration`
- `AutoConfigurationImportSelector` scans `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (Spring Boot 2.7+; older versions used `spring.factories` with the `EnableAutoConfiguration` key)
- Each listed class is a candidate; activation depends on `@ConditionalOn*` guards

**The imports file format**

```
com.example.mylib.MyLibAutoConfiguration
com.example.mylib.MyLibMetricsAutoConfiguration
```

**Common conditionals**
- `@ConditionalOnClass(SomeLib.class)` — library on the classpath
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — user hasn't defined their own
- `@ConditionalOnProperty("myapp.feature.enabled")` — config opts in
- `@ConditionalOnWebApplication` / `@ConditionalOnNotWebApplication`
- `@ConditionalOnBean(SomeOtherBean.class)` — depends on another bean
- `@ConditionalOnSingleCandidate` — exactly one matching bean exists

**Ordering**
- `@AutoConfigureBefore(OtherAutoConfig.class)` — run before another auto-config
- `@AutoConfigureAfter(DataSourceAutoConfig.class)` — run after another
- `@AutoConfigureOrder(Integer)` — explicit numeric ordering

**Tracing what fires**

```properties
logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=conditions
```

- `/actuator/conditions` shows positive matches, negative matches, exclusions, and unconditional classes
- The `--debug` startup flag prints the same report to stdout

**Disabling specific auto-configs**

```java
@SpringBootApplication(exclude = { DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class })
```

```yaml
spring.autoconfigure.exclude: org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration
```

sections.title: Building a Custom Starter — The Two-Module Pattern
Testing with ApplicationContextRunner
AutoConfiguration.imports (Boot 2.7+) vs spring.factories (Boot ≤2.6)
sections.content:
Spring Boot 2.7 introduced a new file format for declaring auto-configurations. Both still work as of Boot 3.x, but the new format is preferred.

| Aspect | spring.factories (≤ Boot 2.6) | AutoConfiguration.imports (Boot 2.7+) |
|---|---|---|
| **Location** | `META-INF/spring.factories` | `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` |
| **Format** | Properties: `key=class1,class2` | One fully-qualified class name per line |
| **Key required** | `org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration=...` | None — file is the key |
| **Spring Boot 3.x** | Still works for legacy starters | Preferred |
| **Recommended class annotation** | `@Configuration` | `@AutoConfiguration` |
| **Conditional ordering** | Manual via `@AutoConfigureBefore`/`After` | Same, plus first-class import-selector ordering |

Use `@AutoConfiguration` (Boot 2.7+) instead of `@Configuration` for auto-config classes — it enables the import-selector machinery, supports inner-class auto-configurations, and produces clearer condition reports.

sections.title: Starter Design Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When custom starters help:**
- Platform team that wants every service to share logging, tracing, metrics, security baselines
- External libraries with optional Spring integration that consumers can opt into
- Repeated configuration boilerplate across multiple services

**When custom starters hurt:**
- Single-service projects — `@Import` of a `@Configuration` class is lighter
- Teams with unfamiliar consumers who can't easily debug auto-config behavior
- Magic that hides important defaults — every auto-configured bean is one a consumer can't easily find

**Watch for:**
- Missing `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — consumer can't override; silent failure mode
- Business classes inside the starter JAR — should live in the autoconfigure or core module
- Forcing dependency versions that conflict with the Boot BOM — consumers can't easily override
- `@Configuration` instead of `@AutoConfiguration` — loses ordering guarantees and import-selector behavior
- Starter pulls heavy transitive deps — `spring-boot-starter-web` adds ~30 jars; bundle thoughtfully
- Conditional evaluation cost at startup — each `@ConditionalOn*` adds milliseconds; many starters together accumulate
- Auto-configuring beans that are always customized — provide a `Customizer<T>` interface instead
- Forgetting `spring-boot-configuration-processor` — IDE shows 'unknown property' warnings for your config

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Starter = empty POM** aggregating dependencies plus transitively pulling autoconfigure JARs and the BOM-pinned versions.
- **`spring-boot-dependencies` BOM** pins transitive versions across all starters so consumers don't manage versions manually.
- **Auto-configuration fires via `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`** in Spring Boot 2.7+; older versions used `spring.factories` with the `EnableAutoConfiguration` key.
- **`@ConditionalOn*` guards** (Class, MissingBean, Property, WebApplication, Bean, SingleCandidate) control activation — get them right and the starter is safe; miss them and the consumer can't override.
- **Custom starter pattern**: `*-spring-boot-autoconfigure` module + `*-spring-boot-starter` empty aggregator module — separation of code from dependency-only artifact.
- **`@ConfigurationProperties` for typed config** — pair with `spring-boot-configuration-processor` for IDE auto-completion of `myprefix.*` keys.
- **Test with `ApplicationContextRunner`** — lightweight, no full Boot context, fast assertions on bean presence and property binding.
- **Use `@AutoConfiguration` (Boot 2.7+) over `@Configuration`** for auto-config classes — supports ordering and import-selector machinery.
- **Debug via `/actuator/conditions`** or `logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG` to see why a bean did or did not appear.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A Spring Boot Starter is an opinionated dependency descriptor — an essentially empty Maven or Gradle artifact that pulls in a curated, version-aligned set of transitive dependencies plus auto-configuration that wires sensible defaults.

**The three roles of a starter**
- Dependency grouping — `spring-boot-starter-web` brings Spring MVC, Jackson, Tomcat, validation
- Version alignment — the `spring-boot-dependencies` BOM pins all transitive versions to a tested combination
- Auto-configuration — starters pull autoconfigure JARs that activate when classes and beans are detected

**How auto-configuration fires**
- `@SpringBootApplication` triggers `@EnableAutoConfiguration`
- Spring scans `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (Boot 2.7+)
- Each listed class becomes a candidate; activates only if `@ConditionalOn*` guards pass
- Common conditionals: `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, `@ConditionalOnProperty`, `@ConditionalOnWebApplication`
- Ordering via `@AutoConfigureBefore`, `@AutoConfigureAfter`, `@AutoConfigureOrder`

**Building a custom starter — the two-module pattern**
- `*-spring-boot-autoconfigure`: contains `@AutoConfiguration` classes, `@ConfigurationProperties`, and the `AutoConfiguration.imports` file
- `*-spring-boot-starter`: empty POM that depends on the core library plus the autoconfigure module
- Consumer adds the starter; conditionals ensure the auto-config activates only when appropriate and steps aside when the consumer defines their own bean

**Best practices for starter authors**
- Always `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` on beans the consumer might override
- Use `@ConditionalOnClass` to guard against missing optional libraries
- `@ConditionalOnProperty(matchIfMissing = true)` for on-by-default opt-out features
- One `@AutoConfiguration` per feature area (main wiring, metrics, health, security)
- Pair `@ConfigurationProperties` with `spring-boot-configuration-processor` for IDE auto-completion
- Test with `ApplicationContextRunner` — no full Boot context needed, super fast

**Debugging a missing bean**
- Enable `logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG` or hit `/actuator/conditions`
- Look at the negative matches section — usually `@ConditionalOnClass` failed, a property is missing, or a bean is already defined

**Format change to know**
- Boot ≤ 2.6: `META-INF/spring.factories` with the `EnableAutoConfiguration` key
- Boot 2.7+: `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`
- Boot 3.x: same file; `@Configuration` deprecated for auto-configs in favor of `@AutoConfiguration`

In an interview, the strong answer is: **starters are empty POMs that aggregate dependencies and trigger auto-configuration; a custom starter is two modules — autoconfigure for the code, starter for the empty aggregator — with `@ConditionalOn*` guards that always let consumers override**.
